overview: This file documents a State Department inquiry into whether Nicholas Basseches, a Russian-born Austrian journalist working in Switzerland, should be permitted or encouraged to accept employment connected with the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun. After the American mission in Bern requested guidance, the Department sought an FBI background check; the FBI found no record under the exact name but supplied potentially relevant information about a similarly named journalist, including associations with a surveilled Washington residence, a vehicle linked to the Japanese Embassy, writings about the Russian Army, and an article praising Stalin in a Cuban publication associated with Communist activity. The Department ultimately replied that it was not in a position to rule on employment by Japanese firms in neutral countries of persons of other foreign nationalities.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Bern declining to rule on employment with Japanese firms
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The State Department declines to decide whether foreign nationals may accept employment with Japanese firms in neutral countries.
subfiles.summary: Replying to telegram 4538 of October 27, the Department states that it is not in a position to pass upon the acceptance of employment with Japanese firms in neutral countries by persons of other foreign nationalities. The secret telegram is signed by Secretary of State Byrnes; the November 13 date is supported by the routing notation on the page.

subfiles.title: Harrison telegram concerning proposed Asahi employment of Basseches
subfiles.about: The American mission in Bern requests guidance on whether journalist Nicholas Basseches may accept a commission from the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports that Nicholas Basseches, described as a Russian-born Austrian national and a well-known journalist who had worked extensively for the pro-Allied weekly Weltwoche in Zurich, wished to accept a commission from Dr. S. Ryu of the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun. Basseches already had the necessary permission from the Swiss foreign police. The mission asks for the Department's attitude; the OCR year “1948” is corrected to 1945 from the file chronology and contemporary filing marks.

subfiles.title: Lyon request to Hoover for information on Basseches
subfiles.from: Frederick B. Lyon, Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.to: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The State Department asks the FBI for information relevant to the proposed appointment of Basseches as the Asahi Shimbun's European representative.
subfiles.summary: Lyon advises Hoover that the American Legation in Bern has reported that a Russian-born Austrian journalist named Nikol Basseches, or a similar first name, wants to become the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun's European representative. The journalist is said to have worked for the Zurich weekly Weltwoche. Lyon requests any available FBI information so the Department can decide whether the proposed appointment would be agreeable.

subfiles.title: Hoover reply concerning Nikol and Nicholas Basseches
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: Hoover reports that the FBI has no record under the exact name Nikol Basseches but has information on a possibly identical Nicholas Basseches.
subfiles.summary: Hoover replies by special messenger that an FBI file review disclosed nothing about Nikol Basseches under that precise identity. The Bureau did, however, possess information about one Nicholas Basseches who might be the same person. Hoover encloses a summary memorandum concerning that individual.

subfiles.title: FBI summary memorandum on Nicholas Basseches
subfiles.about: The enclosure summarizes security-related references, publications, and associations found in FBI files concerning Nicholas Basseches.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes Basseches as the son of a former Austrian consul in Saint Petersburg and notes that he visited a Washington residence under government surveillance; another visitor's automobile was registered to an address care of the Japanese Embassy. It records a New York Times notice of his 1943 book, The Unknown Army, about the Russian Army. It also cites his article “El Hombre de Rusia” in the Havana weekly Nosotros, described as the organ of a cultural organization reputed to be a center of Communist activity, and states that the article praised Stalin.

interest: The file offers a compact example of how the State Department and FBI screened foreign journalists and proposed employees of Japanese institutions immediately after World War II. Particularly useful is the progression from a routine employment inquiry to a security dossier assembled through name matching, surveillance associations, diplomatic connections, and published writings. It also illustrates the uncertainty of such vetting: the FBI could not confirm that its Nicholas Basseches was the same person named by the Bern mission, yet passed along politically suggestive information that could influence the Department's decision.
